title: Kalman filter as an optimal observer

sections.body_md:
The filter gain is not an arbitrary stable observer gain. Among corrections that add a matrix times the innovation, it is the one with the smallest updated error variance. A pole-placed gain can decay quickly and still leave a larger cloud, because decay and variance answer different questions.

The structure that receives the gain is the observer you already know: a copy of the model, plus a correction from the output residual. This skill only changes how the correction is chosen. The intensities \(Q\) and \(R\) replace the hand-written polynomial.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
For a scalar predicted variance \(p\), output coefficient \(c\), and measurement variance \(r\), a trial gain \(L\) leaves the updated variance
\[
(1 - L c)^2 p + L^2 r.
\]
The derivative in \(L\) vanishes at
\[
L = \frac{p c}{c^2 p + r},
\]
and the minimum value equals \((1 - L c) p\). That equality is special to the minimizing gain. A hand-picked gain has to be scored with the two-term expression, or the comparison is dishonest.

In steady state the predicted variance stops moving. The gain freezes, and the copy of the model with that frozen gain is an observer.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take a predicted variance \(2.25\) and a measurement variance \(0.75\), with \(c = 1\). The minimizing gain is \(2.25 / (2.25 + 0.75) = 0.75\). The updated variance is \((1 - 0.75) \times 2.25 = 0.5625\). A guess of \(0.3\) has to be scored as \((1-0.3)^2 \times 2.25 + 0.3^2 \times 0.75\), which is larger. The gap is the whole point of the derivative condition: a nearby gain is legal and worse.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Stability of \(A - L C\) does not freeze the variance. Every stable gain has its own cloud. Using the simplified product \((1-Lc)p\) on a gain that did not come from the formula understates that gain's variance, because the simplified product has already used the optimality condition to cancel a term. Swapping the names \(Q\) and \(R\) with the weights of a quadratic regulator produces a similar-looking equation and a different gain. The regulator penalizes the command. This design describes the noise.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The gain from this page can be placed next to a state-feedback gain that was chosen for the regulator poles or for a quadratic cost. The two gains do not have to be equal. A later combined command uses both, and a constraint on the actuator is a different problem again: a variance formula will not enforce a hard bound. A horizon that carries the bound explicitly is the design that does.
